sections.title: Symptoms and signs of pleural effusion

blocks.text: Pleuritic pain (sharp, worse on breathing in and coughing) and a **pleural rub** often come first, especially when the effusion follows pneumonia, pulmonary infarction or connective tissue disease. If **breathlessness** is the only complaint, the onset can be gradual: how a patient presents depends on the **volume** of fluid and **how fast** it has collected. Small effusions are often silent.

blocks.title: Examination findings on the side of a large effusion
rows: Tachypnoea; reduced chest expansion on the affected side
Usually central; pushed **away** from the effusion only when it is massive
**Stony dull** over the fluid (mid and lower zones)
Reduced or absent over the fluid
Bronchial breathing or crackles from compressed lung

blocks.text: About **500 mL** of fluid is needed before an effusion can be found clinically, so a small effusion may show on imaging with a normal examination.

With healthy lungs a moderate effusion is well tolerated, but in someone with existing lung disease the same effusion can tip them into **respiratory failure**. Orthopnoea, oedema and other features of heart failure point to a cardiac cause.

Both an effusion and a pneumothorax give **reduced breath sounds**. The **percussion note** separates them: stony dull means fluid, while a resonant or hyper-resonant note with absent breath sounds means air.

blocks.note: Look at: the large right pleural effusion panel. Compare its signs with pneumothorax, collapse and consolidation, and note the effusion hiding the right heart border on the X-ray inset.

sections.title: Imaging: chest X-ray, ultrasound and CT

blocks.title: Chest X-ray
items: Erect PA film: a **curved basal shadow** that blunts the costophrenic angle and climbs toward the axilla (the **meniscus**).
The fluid actually surrounds the lung. It only shows where the X-ray beam passes tangentially through it at the lateral chest wall.
About **200 mL** is needed before fluid shows on a PA film (Davidson).
A **subpulmonary** collection under the lower lobe looks like a raised hemidiaphragm.
Fluid trapped in an **oblique fissure** can form a round opacity that is mistaken for a tumour.
A massive effusion can push the trachea and mediastinum to the other side.

blocks.text: **Ultrasound** finds pleural fluid more accurately than a plain film, picks up small effusions and is used to **guide aspiration**. **CT** is indicated when malignancy is suspected. A **contrast-enhanced CT** done while fluid is still present shows pleural thickening or nodules best and guides needle biopsy. In empyema, ultrasound or CT is used to choose the aspiration site.

Sources disagree on the minimum volume visible on chest X-ray: **about 200 mL** in Davidson, 250 mL in Step-Up and 300 mL in Kumar & Clark and Clinical Medicine Essentials. For exams, use Davidson's figure of **~200 mL**. Clinical detection needs about 500 mL.

blocks.note: Look at: blunting of the right costophrenic angle from a small right effusion (A), and a left pleural effusion (B).
Look at: echo-free (black) fluid above the diaphragm and the "spine sign": the spine is visible through the fluid, which does not happen through aerated lung.
Look at: a dense, homogeneous shadow over part of the hemithorax with a meniscus on the erect film, alongside the listed bedside signs.

sections.title: Pleural aspiration (thoracocentesis), fluid analysis and biopsy

blocks.text: **Most new effusions need a diagnostic tap.** The exception is a typical effusion in **left ventricular failure**: treat it (diuretics) and re-assess. Tap only if there are atypical features, such as a markedly asymmetric effusion, fever, pleuritic pain or failure to resolve. The tap is usually **ultrasound-guided**, done with aseptic technique under local anaesthetic. Small effusions and failed blind attempts always need image guidance.

blocks.title: Light's criteria: exudate if ANY one is met
rows: Above 2/3 of the reference upper limit for serum LDH

blocks.text: A quick bedside rule is fluid protein **< 30 g/L = transudate** and **> 30 g/L = exudate**. Use Light's criteria, with a paired venous protein and LDH, when fluid protein is 25–35 g/L or the serum protein is abnormal.

blocks.title: What to send and what it tells you
rows: Pus means empyema, milky fluid means chylothorax, and blood suggests infarction or malignancy (or a traumatic tap)
Low in infection/empyema; also in RA, oesophageal rupture and advanced malignancy
Cytology is essential. Lymphocytes suggest TB, malignancy or rheumatoid disease; neutrophils suggest parapneumonic effusion, PE or pancreatitis

blocks.title: Useful pleural fluid clues
rows: Very low glucose (± cholesterol in chronic effusion)
Rheumatoid arthritis (also empyema, TB, malignancy, SLE, oesophageal rupture)
Fluid amylase higher than serum amylase
Acute pancreatitis; also oesophageal rupture or malignancy
Blood or air in the pleural space, drugs, asbestos

blocks.text: If aspiration does not give a diagnosis, get a contrast CT, then tissue: **image-guided (US/CT) pleural biopsy**, a blind Abrams needle biopsy, or **video-assisted thoracoscopy (VATS)**. VATS lets the operator see the pleura, take targeted biopsies and drain the effusion in one procedure. Tissue goes for histology and TB culture.

Light's criteria are very sensitive (~97%) but less specific (~85%). They label about **a quarter of transudates as exudates**, typically heart-failure effusions after diuresis ("pseudoexudate"). Pocket Medicine lists a serum-minus-effusion albumin gradient **≤ 1.2** as a more specific exudate criterion, so a gradient **above 1.2 g/dL**, or a pleural NT-proBNP ≥ 1500 pg/mL, still favours a heart-failure transudate.

**Negative cytology does not exclude cancer.** In TB the fluid holds few organisms: fluid culture is positive in only about 20% of cases, compared with about 80% for pleural biopsy. Biopsy is often needed.

**Transudates** are caused by systemic factors: raised hydrostatic pressure or reduced oncotic pressure (cardiac, liver or renal failure). The pleura itself is normal. **Exudates** are caused by local factors: leaky capillaries from disease of the pleura or adjacent lung, or blocked lymphatic drainage.

blocks.title: Causes by fluid type
rows: Rare: drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin), benign asbestos effusion, sarcoidosis, yellow nail syndrome

blocks.title: Classic patterns (Davidson Box 17.13)
rows: Raised ADA; positive tuberculin test; culture +ve ~20%, biopsy +ve ~80%
Malignant cell clumps; biopsy +ve ~40%; primary elsewhere
Other signs of failure; responds to diuretics
Usually an exudate, clear or bloody; occasionally a transudate
Eosinophils and red cells; a DVT or other embolic source
Very low glucose; cholesterol in chronic effusion; RF/anti-CCP

blocks.text: **Heart failure** causes about 40% of all effusions and is bilateral in most cases. **Massive** effusions are most often **malignant**. Among malignant causes, lung cancer leads (~36%), followed by breast (~25%) and lymphoma (~10%).
In an **elderly patient with a unilateral effusion**, always consider TB and actively exclude it.
Rheumatoid effusions are usually **unilateral and chronic**, with low glucose. Lupus causes pleurisy in up to two-thirds of patients, and any effusion is usually **small and bilateral**.

**PE** is listed under both headings: the effusion is usually an exudate, often blood-stained, with pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and a rub, but it can occasionally be a transudate. **Hepatic hydrothorax** is usually right-sided and can be large even with little ascites. A nephrotic patient with a new effusion still needs PE excluded.

**Treat the cause** (heart failure, pneumonia, PE, subphrenic abscess) and the effusion often resolves. **Transudates** are managed by treating the underlying disease (e.g. diuretics and salt restriction), with therapeutic aspiration only for a massive effusion causing breathlessness. **Exudates** more often need a specific pleural procedure. An empyema must be drained.

blocks.title: Therapeutic aspiration and drainage
items: Aspiration relieves breathlessness, but the effusion may come back. A chest drain empties it more completely.
Removing **more than 1.5 L at once** carries a risk of **re-expansion pulmonary oedema** (Davidson).
Kumar's drain protocol: ultrasound-guided Seldinger drain on an underwater seal, removing about 1 L at a time and then clamping. Stop if the patient becomes uncomfortable.
Drain slowly: a rapid shift of the mediastinum causes severe pain and occasionally shock.

blocks.text: **Never drain an effusion to dryness before you have a diagnosis.** Without fluid, a pleural biopsy may not be possible until the effusion builds up again.

blocks.title: Recurrent malignant effusion
rows: Do it only if the lung **fully re-expands**; about 80–90% success
Fewer days in hospital, but more adverse events
Relief is temporary; the fluid re-accumulates

blocks.text: Some sources (Kumar, Clinical Medicine Essentials) describe aspirating a malignant effusion "to dryness" before instilling talc, tetracycline or bleomycin. Davidson stresses drainage by intercostal tube, with talc pleurodesis **only if the lung fully re-expands**. Follow Davidson. **Pleural pH < 7.2** and **systemic steroids** predict that pleurodesis will fail.

blocks.title: Specific situations
items: **TB effusion:** often settles on its own, but the patient still needs a full course of anti-TB treatment. Glucocorticoids may help pleural TB.
**Hepatic hydrothorax:** control the ascites. **Avoid chest tubes.** Options are repeated taps, pleurodesis, TIPS or surgical repair, and transplant is definitive.
**Parapneumonic effusion / empyema:** see the next section.

blocks.text: More than **40%** of community-acquired pneumonias produce a **parapneumonic effusion**, and about **15%** of those become infected, forming an **empyema** (Kumar quotes one-third to one-half of CAP for the effusion). The process moves from a sterile exudate, to an infected fibrinopurulent stage with loculations, to **organisation**, where a rigid fibrous peel traps the lung. Other routes to empyema include an infected haemothorax after trauma or surgery, oesophageal rupture and a subphrenic abscess bursting through the diaphragm.

blocks.title: When to suspect empyema
items: Pneumonia that is improving but has **persistent or recurrent fever** despite appropriate antibiotics
Severe pleuritic pain
High remittent fever, rigors, sweats, weight loss
**Neutrophil leucocytosis** and a high CRP
CXR: an effusion, or a **D-shaped** pleural-based opacity when adhesions loculate the pus

blocks.title: Pleural fluid features of empyema / complicated effusion
rows: Pus or positive Gram stain / culture

blocks.text: The pH cut-off depends on the source: **pH < 7.0** for empyema in Davidson, **< 7.2** for a complicated parapneumonic effusion in US texts, and **< 7.3** "suggests infection" in Clinical Medicine Essentials. Davidson is the primary source for exams. **Never put thick pus in a blood-gas analyser**, because it damages the machine.

blocks.title: Treating empyema (Davidson)
items: A **wide-bore intercostal tube** in the most dependent part of the cavity
If the fluid is turbid, frank pus or loculated: suction at +5 to +10 cmH2O and regular 20 mL saline flushes
Antibiotics for **2–4 weeks**, targeted if the organism is known. If it is unknown: IV co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime plus metronidazole
If the drain fails (thick or loculated pus): **surgery** to clear the cavity and break down adhesions
**Decortication** for a thick visceral peel that stops the lung re-expanding. Surgery is also needed for a bronchopleural fistula

blocks.text: Davidson states that **intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy is of no benefit** in empyema. Step-Up uses intrapleural alteplase (tPA) and dornase (DNase) when a complicated effusion drains poorly through a chest tube, and Pocket Medicine says tPA plus DNase reduces the need for surgery. Follow Davidson, but recognise the alternative view.

blocks.title: Complications of an untreated empyema
items: Rupture into a bronchus: **bronchopleural fistula** with pyopneumothorax (air-fluid level) and sudden copious purulent sputum
Tracking through the chest wall: **empyema necessitans** (subcutaneous abscess or sinus)
A thick pleural rind, a long hospital admission and higher mortality

blocks.title: Complications of thoracocentesis and drainage
rows: Commonest: about 5–15% of taps, under 3% with ultrasound guidance; few need a drain
Risk when > 1.5 L is removed at once
From a tap placed too low
Pain or shock from mediastinal shift
From draining a large effusion too fast

blocks.note: Look at: the D-shaped shadow in the left mid-zone, a loculated empyema that persists despite an intercostal drain.
Look at: septations crossing the fluid on pleural ultrasound, as in a multiloculated empyema.

blocks.title: What is in the pleural space?
rows: Fluid : blood haematocrit > 50%; can become infected
Thoracic duct leak from trauma/surgery or carcinoma; also lymphangioleiomyomatosis; triglycerides high, chylomicrons
Primary (no lung disease) or secondary (e.g. COPD)

blocks.text: **Pleurisy** is pleural inflammation without much fluid. It causes sharp pain on breathing and coughing. Causes include pneumonia, pulmonary infarction and carcinoma. **Bornholm disease** (Coxsackie B) follows an upper respiratory infection with pleuritic and abdominal pain and tender muscles. The CXR stays normal, and it settles within about a week.

blocks.title: Asbestos-related pleural disease
rows: Commonest sign of past exposure. Hyaline fibrosis of the parietal pleura, often calcified ("candle wax"). Asymptomatic, benign, no effect on lung function
Diagnosis of exclusion. Biopsy may be needed to exclude mesothelioma
Visceral pleura; blunts the costophrenic angles; can cause a **restrictive** defect; no specific treatment
Long latency after exposure. Breathlessness from effusion or unremitting chest wall pain. Poor prognosis; palliative care with drainage and pleurodesis

blocks.title: Pneumothorax essentials
items: **Primary:** no lung disease; tall, thin young men and smokers; apical blebs. **Secondary:** underlying lung disease, most often COPD; higher mortality.

Primary, rim < 2 cm and not breathless: usually resolves without intervention. Breathless or larger: needle aspiration (16F cannula, 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line; stop after 2.5 L), then a drain if that fails.
Secondary: admit. Usually needs a chest drain, especially if over 50 or with respiratory compromise.

**Tension pneumothorax:** marked tachycardia, hypotension, cyanosis and the trachea pushed **away** from a silent, hyper-resonant side. **Decompress immediately** without waiting for imaging, then insert a drain (4th–6th intercostal space, mid-axillary line).

blocks.note: Look at: extensive calcified pleural plaques on the diaphragm and lateral chest wall with a "candle wax" outline.
Look at: the spontaneous pneumothorax algorithm: when to observe, aspirate or insert a drain, and the immediate decompression of a tension pneumothorax.
Look at: the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. A rim over 2 cm means a large pneumothorax.

cards.front: Percussion note over a large pleural effusion?
cards.back: **Stony dull**, with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the fluid

cards.front: Absent breath sounds: which percussion note means pneumothorax rather than effusion?
cards.back: Resonant or hyper-resonant. Stony dullness means fluid

cards.front: When is the trachea pushed away from an effusion?
Minimum pleural fluid visible on an erect PA chest X-ray (Davidson)?
cards.back: About **200 mL**. Clinical detection needs about 500 mL

cards.front: What does a subpulmonary effusion mimic on CXR?

cards.back: An evolving **empyema** or a resolving haemothorax
Any one of: fluid/serum protein > 0.5; fluid/serum LDH > 0.6; fluid LDH > two-thirds of the ULN of serum LDH

cards.front: Which effusion can usually be treated before it is sampled?
cards.back: A typical effusion in **left ventricular failure**. Treat, re-assess, and tap only if atypical

cards.front: TB effusion: fluid culture yield vs pleural biopsy yield?
cards.back: Culture is positive in about 20%; biopsy in about 80%. Adenosine deaminase is raised
An ovarian tumour (fibroma) with a **right-sided** transudative effusion (± ascites)

cards.front: Effusion with very low glucose and cholesterol in a chronic exudate?
Volume above which therapeutic aspiration risks re-expansion pulmonary oedema?
cards.back: More than **1.5 L** at one time

cards.front: Why not drain an undiagnosed effusion to dryness?
cards.back: A pleural biopsy may then be impossible until fluid re-accumulates

cards.front: Davidson pleural fluid features suggesting empyema?
cards.back: Pus; glucose < 3.3 mmol/L; LDH > 1000 IU/L; pH < 7.0

cards.front: Empyema antibiotics when the organism is unknown (Davidson)?
cards.back: IV co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime plus metronidazole, for 2–4 weeks with drainage
Chylothorax: thoracic duct leak (trauma or carcinoma)

cards.front: Commonest pleural sign of past asbestos exposure?
cards.back: Pleural plaques: benign, asymptomatic, no effect on lung function

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has had worsening breathlessness for 3 weeks. At the right base there is reduced expansion, a stony dull percussion note, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. The trachea is central.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance is the classic triad over pleural fluid. The trachea stays central unless the effusion is massive.
whyNot: A pneumothorax gives a resonant or hyper-resonant note, not stony dullness.
Consolidation is dull, but breath sounds are bronchial and vocal resonance is increased.
Collapse is dull, but the trachea is pulled toward the affected side.
Fibrosis gives fine inspiratory crackles at the bases, not absent breath sounds over a stony dull area.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has breathlessness and markedly reduced breath sounds over the left hemithorax. You must decide at the bedside whether this is air or fluid.
questions.leadIn: Which single examination finding best makes the distinction?
questions.explanation: Both air and fluid reduce breath sounds and expansion. Percussion separates them: stony dull over fluid, resonant or hyper-resonant over air.
whyNot: Breath sounds are reduced in both conditions.
Expansion is reduced on the affected side in both.
Tachypnoea is non-specific.
The trachea is pushed away in both a massive effusion and a tension pneumothorax, so its position does not discriminate.

questions.stem: A medical student reviews an erect PA chest X-ray that shows only minimal blunting of the left costophrenic angle.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, approximately how much pleural fluid must be present before it can be seen on a PA film?
questions.explanation: Davidson quotes about 200 mL as the volume needed for a PA film to show fluid. Other texts quote 250–300 mL, but Davidson is the primary source for exams.
whyNot: Far too little to show on a PA film; ultrasound can detect small volumes.
500 mL is the approximate volume needed for clinical detection, not radiological detection.
This would give an obvious large shadow, not just angle blunting.
1.5 L is the threshold linked to re-expansion oedema during aspiration, not detection.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is recovering from a right lower lobe pneumonia. Pleural ultrasound shows fluid divided by multiple fibrinous strands.
questions.leadIn: What does this appearance most strongly suggest?
questions.explanation: Septations most likely indicate an evolving empyema (or a resolving haemothorax). After pneumonia, empyema is the concern.
whyNot: A transudate usually appears as a clear echo-free space.
A hydrothorax is a transudate and is typically echo-free.
Hypoalbuminaemic effusions are transudates without septations.
A subpulmonary collection is a location, not an ultrasound texture; a transudate would be echo-free.

questions.stem: Pleural fluid and paired serum are analysed in a patient with a new unilateral effusion.
questions.leadIn: Which single result is enough on its own to classify the effusion as an exudate by Light's criteria?
options: Pleural LDH one-third of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural glucose equal to serum glucose
questions.explanation: Any one Light's criterion is enough: protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or fluid LDH > two-thirds of the ULN of serum LDH. An LDH ratio of 0.7 meets the second criterion.
whyNot: A protein ratio of 0.4 is below the 0.5 cut-off.
One-third of the ULN is below the two-thirds threshold.
Glucose is not part of Light's criteria.
Appearance is not a Light's criterion; straw-coloured fluid is typical of a transudate.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with known heart failure has bilateral effusions after several days of IV furosemide. A tap of the larger side shows a fluid : serum protein ratio of 0.53. LDH criteria are not met. Clinically everything fits heart failure.
questions.leadIn: Which additional result would best support the effusion still being a transudate?
options: Pleural fluid amylase above serum amylase
questions.explanation: Light's criteria misclassify about a quarter of transudates, classically after diuresis concentrates the protein ("pseudoexudate"). A high serum–effusion albumin gradient (or a high pleural NT-proBNP) still supports heart failure.
whyNot: A high ADA suggests tuberculosis.
A raised fluid amylase points to pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture.
High triglycerides indicate chylothorax.
Pleural eosinophilia suggests blood or air in the pleural space, drugs or asbestos.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has symmetrical deforming arthritis of the small joints of the hands and positive anti-CCP antibodies. She has had a right-sided effusion for 5 months. The fluid is a turbid exudate with very low glucose and raised cholesterol.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the effusion?
questions.explanation: A chronic, unilateral exudate with very low glucose and cholesterol in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis is the classic rheumatoid effusion.
whyNot: Lupus effusions are usually small and bilateral, and anti-CCP points to rheumatoid arthritis.
Heart-failure effusions are straw-coloured transudates, usually bilateral.
Nephrotic effusions are transudates from hypoalbuminaemia.
Meigs' syndrome is a transudate linked to an ovarian tumour.

questions.stem: You are asked to list causes of a transudative pleural effusion.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following typically produces a transudate?
questions.explanation: Myxoedema is a recognised transudate cause alongside heart failure, hypoproteinaemia, constrictive pericarditis and Meigs' syndrome.
whyNot: TB causes a lymphocytic exudate.
Malignancy causes an exudate, often blood-stained.
Pancreatitis causes an exudate with a high fluid amylase.
Post-MI (Dressler) syndrome is an inflammatory, exudative cause.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a recurrent, symptomatic right pleural effusion. After drainage through an intercostal tube, the chest X-ray shows the lung has fully re-expanded.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step to prevent recurrence?
questions.explanation: For a malignant effusion, drain by intercostal tube, and if the lung fully re-expands, instil a sclerosant such as talc (pleurodesis) to stop the fluid re-accumulating.
whyNot: Repeated aspiration gives only temporary relief.
Fibrinolytics are used for loculated infection, not to prevent malignant recurrence.
Decortication is for a thick fibrous peel trapping the lung, as in chronic empyema.
Diuretics treat transudates; a malignant effusion is an exudate.

questions.stem: A breathless 70-year-old man is having therapeutic aspiration of a large effusion. The registrar warns against removing too much fluid at one sitting.
questions.leadIn: Removing more than about 1.5 L at once particularly risks which complication?
questions.explanation: Davidson links removal of more than 1.5 L at a time with a small risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
whyNot: Chylothorax results from a thoracic duct leak, not from the volume aspirated.
Empyema necessitans is pus tracking through the chest wall.
Pleural plaques reflect asbestos exposure.
Meigs' syndrome is an ovarian tumour with an effusion.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man is on day 6 of IV antibiotics for right lower lobe pneumonia. He still has fever spikes and severe right pleuritic pain. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yields turbid fluid with glucose 2.0 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wide-bore intercostal drain plus continued antibiotics
Switch to oral antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
questions.explanation: Persistent fever despite antibiotics with turbid, low-glucose fluid means empyema. It must be drained with a wide-bore tube, with antibiotics continued for 2–4 weeks.
whyNot: An empyema will not resolve on antibiotics alone; the cavity must be drained.
Diuretics treat transudates.
Pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant effusion, not infection.
Waiting allows organisation into a thick peel or a bronchopleural fistula.

questions.stem: Pleural fluid from a febrile patient with a resolving pneumonia is analysed.
questions.leadIn: Which result does Davidson list as a feature suggesting empyema?
questions.explanation: Davidson's pointers to empyema are frank pus, glucose < 3.3 mmol/L, LDH > 1000 IU/L and pH < 7.0.
whyNot: A normal glucose argues against empyema.
A normal pH argues against empyema.
A low protein ratio suggests a transudate.
Straw-coloured clear fluid suggests a transudate, not pus.

questions.stem: Five days after an oesophagectomy, a 64-year-old man has a large right effusion. Aspiration yields milky white fluid with very high triglycerides and chylomicrons.
questions.leadIn: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Milky fluid containing chylomicrons is chyle. It comes from thoracic duct damage, here caused by surgery.
whyNot: Empyema is pus with neutrophils and a low pH and glucose, not chylomicrons.
Haemothorax is blood, with a fluid : blood haematocrit > 50%.
Hepatic hydrothorax is a clear transudate in cirrhosis.
A malignant effusion is usually a blood-stained exudate with malignant cells.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old retired shipyard worker has a routine chest X-ray showing calcified, irregular pleural opacities along the diaphragm with a "candle wax" outline. He has no symptoms, and spirometry and gas transfer are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Calcified "candle wax" plaques in an asymptomatic person with normal lung function are pleural plaques, the commonest sign of past asbestos exposure.
whyNot: Mesothelioma presents with effusion or unremitting chest wall pain.
Diffuse thickening affects the visceral pleura, blunts the costophrenic angles and can restrict lung function.
This would show fluid, not calcified plaques.
Asbestosis is parenchymal fibrosis with crackles and restriction.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has lost weight over the past 2 months and has a left pleural effusion. The fluid is a lymphocytic exudate with raised adenosine deaminase. AFB smear and cytology are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most useful next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Image-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy for histology and culture
questions.explanation: TB is likely (elderly, unilateral, lymphocytic exudate, raised ADA), but organisms in the fluid are sparse. Fluid culture is positive in only ~20%, while pleural biopsy (histology and culture) is positive in ~80%.
whyNot: Fluid smears have a very low yield in TB.
Diuretics treat transudates.
Pleurodesis before a diagnosis is inappropriate.
Amylase helps only if pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture is suspected.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has abdominal distension. Pelvic ultrasound shows a solid ovarian mass, and there is ascites. Chest X-ray shows a right pleural effusion, which is a transudate.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An ovarian tumour (classically a fibroma) with ascites and a right-sided transudative effusion is Meigs' syndrome.
whyNot: TB gives a lymphocytic exudate.
Constrictive pericarditis causes transudates, but there is no ovarian mass.
Nephrotic effusions are usually bilateral, with heavy proteinuria.
Pancreatitis causes an exudate with a high amylase.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with heavy alcohol use has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a small left effusion. Fluid amylase is higher than serum amylase, and no cell type predominates.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the effusion?
questions.explanation: Davidson lists acute pancreatitis as a serous or blood-stained exudate in which fluid amylase exceeds serum amylase.
whyNot: Rheumatoid effusions are characterised by very low glucose.
Heart failure gives a transudate with normal amylase.
Infarction gives red cells and eosinophils, with an embolic source.
TB gives a lymphocytic exudate with a raised ADA.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old smoker has progressive breathlessness. The chest X-ray shows complete opacification of the left hemithorax, with the trachea and mediastinum displaced to the right.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Massive effusions are most often malignant (lung, breast and lymphoma lead the list). A smoker with a massive unilateral effusion pushing the mediastinum away fits this.
whyNot: Heart-failure effusions are bilateral in about 80% of cases, which does not fit a massive one-sided effusion in a smoker.
Nephrotic effusions are small and bilateral.
Hypothyroidism is an uncommon transudate cause; a massive unilateral effusion is most often malignant.
Collapse pulls the trachea toward the affected side.

questions.stem: Several patients with pleural effusions are reviewed on the ward round.
questions.leadIn: In which patient is it reasonable to treat first and defer diagnostic pleural aspiration?
options: A 78-year-old with orthopnoea, raised JVP, bilateral basal effusions and cardiomegaly
A 70-year-old ex-smoker with weight loss and a unilateral effusion
A 40-year-old with pneumonia, a new effusion and persistent fever
A 33-year-old with night sweats and a unilateral effusion
A 60-year-old with lupus and a unilateral effusion with pleuritic pain and fever
questions.explanation: In typical left ventricular failure the effusion need not be sampled. Treat, re-evaluate, and tap only if atypical features appear. Nearly all other effusions need diagnostic aspiration.
whyNot: A unilateral effusion with weight loss raises suspicion of malignancy and needs sampling.
A parapneumonic effusion with persistent fever needs urgent sampling to exclude empyema.
A possible TB effusion needs fluid analysis and probably biopsy.
Fever and pleuritic pain are atypical features that need sampling, even with a known cause.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the right chest. He is cyanosed, with pulse 140/min, BP 75/40 mmHg, the trachea deviated to the left, and a hyper-resonant, silent right hemithorax.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Immediate decompression with a cannula into the right pleural space
Urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
Diagnostic pleural aspiration for protein and LDH
questions.explanation: These are the signs of a tension pneumothorax. Release the pressure immediately with a cannula, then insert a chest drain. Do not wait for imaging.
whyNot: Waiting for imaging in tension pneumothorax risks cardiac arrest.
This is air, not fluid, and he is in extremis.
Pleurodesis has no role in acute management.
The picture is not PE; delay is dangerous.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has a confirmed empyema after aspiration pneumonia. A wide-bore drain is in place, and cultures have grown no organism.
questions.leadIn: Which empirical antibiotic regimen does Davidson suggest?
options: No antibiotic, as drainage alone is sufficient
questions.explanation: When the organism is unknown, Davidson suggests IV co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime plus metronidazole, given for 2–4 weeks alongside drainage.
whyNot: Not the suggested regimen, and far shorter than the 2–4 weeks needed.
Not a recommended empirical regimen for empyema.
5 days is far shorter than the 2–4 weeks needed.
Empyema needs both drainage and prolonged antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old former insulation worker has a new unilateral exudative effusion. Aspirate cytology is negative, and a benign asbestos effusion is suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis must be actively excluded before accepting that label?
questions.explanation: Benign asbestos pleurisy is a diagnosis of exclusion. A biopsy may be needed to rule out mesothelioma, which also follows asbestos exposure and presents with effusion.
whyNot: Plaques do not cause effusions or symptoms.
Heart failure gives a transudate, not an exudate.
Meigs' syndrome gives a transudate with an ovarian tumour.
A pneumothorax is air, not an exudate.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has a unilateral effusion. Pleural fluid: protein 35 g/L, LDH 260 IU/L. Serum: protein 70 g/L, LDH 300 IU/L. The upper limit of normal for serum LDH is 250 IU/L.
questions.leadIn: How should this effusion be classified?
questions.explanation: Work through Light's criteria one at a time. **Step 1, protein ratio:** 35/70 = 0.50. The criterion needs **> 0.5**, so it is **not** met. **Step 2, LDH ratio:** 260/300 = 0.87, which is > 0.6, so it **is** met. **Step 3, absolute LDH:** two-thirds of 250 is about 167, and 260 > 167, so this is also met. Because **any one** criterion defines an exudate, this effusion is an **exudate**. Do not stop after the protein ratio. The quick 30 g/L protein rule is not reliable here either, because 35 g/L sits in the 25–35 g/L zone where Light's criteria should be applied.
whyNot: A transudate must meet none of the criteria; two are met here.
Chylous effusions are identified by milky fluid and triglycerides, not by Light's criteria.
Haemothorax is defined by the fluid haematocrit.
pH is not part of Light's criteria.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted with left lower lobe pneumonia. On day 7 of appropriate IV antibiotics his fever has returned, his CRP is rising and he has rigors. The chest X-ray shows a D-shaped, pleural-based opacity in the left mid-zone.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to a different antibiotic class and observe
questions.explanation: **Step 1, recognise the pattern:** recurrent fever and rising inflammatory markers despite appropriate antibiotics should make you suspect empyema. **Step 2, read the film:** a D-shaped opacity against the chest wall is pus loculated by adhesions. **Step 3, confirm and plan:** use ultrasound (or CT) to choose the site, then aspirate, ideally with a wide-bore needle. Thick or turbid pus confirms empyema, as do glucose < 3.3 mmol/L, LDH > 1000 IU/L or pH < 7.0. **Step 4, treat:** a wide-bore intercostal drain plus 2–4 weeks of antibiotics, with surgery if drainage fails.
whyNot: Changing antibiotics alone leaves the pus undrained.
PE is not suggested; the picture is a pleural collection.
Bronchoscopy does not diagnose or drain a pleural collection.
Pleurodesis is for malignant effusion and is contraindicated in infection.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old ex-smoker has a 6-week history of breathlessness and a moderate right effusion. The first aspirate is a lymphocytic exudate, and cytology shows no malignant cells. The team plans the next step.
questions.leadIn: Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT while fluid is still present, then image-guided or thoracoscopic biopsy
Drain the effusion to dryness with a chest tube, then reassess
Discharge, as negative cytology excludes malignancy
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** negative cytology does **not** exclude malignancy, and TB is also possible in an older patient with a unilateral lymphocytic exudate. **Step 2:** get contrast-enhanced CT while fluid remains, because the contrast between fluid and pleura shows thickening or nodules best. **Step 3:** take tissue by US/CT-guided biopsy or VATS, which also allows drainage. **Key pitfall:** never drain to dryness before a diagnosis, because biopsy may then be impossible.
whyNot: Draining to dryness before a diagnosis can make biopsy impossible.
Cytology can be negative in a malignant effusion.
Pleurodesis before a tissue diagnosis is premature.
An exudate is not treated with diuretics.

questions.theme: Causes of pleural effusion from fluid findings
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most appropriate option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man recently arrived from a TB-endemic region has 6 weeks of night sweats and a right effusion. The fluid is an amber exudate with mostly lymphocytes, and the adenosine deaminase is markedly raised.
items.explanation: An amber, lymphocytic exudate with a raised ADA is typical of TB. A pleural biopsy gives the highest yield.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man develops sudden severe lower chest pain after a bout of forceful vomiting. A left effusion has a low pH and an amylase level well above normal.
items.explanation: This needs two steps. A low pH alone could mean infection, and a high amylase alone could mean pancreatitis. Together, after vomiting, they point to oesophageal rupture (salivary amylase leaks into the pleura).

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman, 10 days after hip surgery, has sudden pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and a pleural rub. There is a small, blood-stained exudative effusion with red cells and eosinophils.
items.explanation: A post-operative patient with pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and a small blood-stained exudate fits pulmonary infarction from PE.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman has orthopnoea, bilateral ankle oedema and a raised JVP. She has bilateral straw-coloured effusions that shrink with diuretics.
items.explanation: Bilateral, straw-coloured transudates that respond to diuretics are typical of heart failure, the commonest cause overall.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most appropriate option from the list. Any option can fit one case, several cases, or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a small left effusion. A bedside "blind" diagnostic tap has failed twice.
items.explanation: Small effusions and failed blind taps need image guidance, usually ultrasound.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a recurrent unilateral exudate. Two cytology samples and a CT-guided biopsy are non-diagnostic, and CT shows pleural nodularity. The team wants direct inspection, targeted biopsy and drainage in one procedure.
items.explanation: VATS lets the operator see the pleura, take targeted biopsies and drain the fluid, all in one procedure.

items.stem: Two days after a thoracotomy, milky fluid is draining from a 59-year-old man's chest tube.
items.explanation: Milky fluid suggests chylothorax. High triglycerides (> 110 mg/dL) and chylomicrons confirm it.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a lymphocytic exudate. AFB smear is negative, and the team wants a quick fluid test that supports a mycobacterial cause.
items.explanation: A raised ADA (> 70) supports TB, while a low value (< 40) argues against it. Biopsy remains the highest-yield test.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has a pleural effusion on chest X-ray, but chest examination is unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: According to Kumar & Clark, roughly how much fluid is usually needed before an effusion is detectable clinically?
questions.explanation: Kumar & Clark and Clinical Medicine Essentials give about 500 mL for clinical detection, which is more than the volume visible on a chest X-ray.
whyNot: Too small to produce signs.
About 200 mL is Davidson's figure for visibility on a PA X-ray.
1.5 L is the re-expansion oedema threshold for aspiration.
2.5 L is the cut-off for stopping aspiration of a pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with lupus has fever, polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain.
questions.leadIn: Which pleural finding is most typical of SLE?
options: Very low glucose with high cholesterol in a chronic unilateral effusion
questions.explanation: Pleurisy affects up to two-thirds of patients with SLE, and any effusion is usually small and bilateral.
whyNot: A massive blood-stained effusion suggests malignancy.
This describes chylothorax.
Frank pus is empyema.
This is the rheumatoid arthritis pattern.

questions.stem: A ward team audits the causes of pleural effusions in their hospital.
questions.leadIn: Which condition is the single most common cause of pleural effusion?
questions.explanation: Heart failure is the commonest cause, accounting for roughly 40% of effusions, and is usually bilateral.
whyNot: TB is an important exudate cause, especially in endemic areas, but less common overall.
Malignancy is a leading cause of exudates and of massive effusions.
PE is a less common cause, at about 10%.
Rheumatoid effusions are uncommon.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has an empyema with a wide-bore drain on suction and regular saline flushes. After a week of appropriate antibiotics the pus remains thick and loculated, and the lung has not re-expanded.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Surgical clearance of the cavity, with decortication if a thick peel traps the lung
Remove the drain and continue oral antibiotics
questions.explanation: When the tube drains inadequately (thick or loculated pus), Davidson recommends surgery to clear the pus and break down adhesions, with decortication for a thick visceral peel. Davidson states that intrapleural fibrinolytics give no benefit, although some US texts use tPA plus DNase.
whyNot: Davidson states fibrinolytics are of no benefit.
Undrained pus will persist and may organise or form a fistula.
Pleurodesis is contraindicated in active infection.
A narrower tube drains thick pus less well.

questions.stem: A consent discussion for diagnostic thoracocentesis is taking place.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is the most common?
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is the commonest complication (about 5–15%, under 3% with ultrasound guidance). Few patients need a drain.
whyNot: This occurs only with large-volume removal (> 1.5 L) and is uncommon.
This is rare and is avoided by not tapping too low.
This occurs in only about 1%.
This is a complication of untreated empyema, not of a tap.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old tall, thin man has sudden left pleuritic pain. He is not breathless. The chest X-ray shows a primary spontaneous pneumothorax with a rim of 1.5 cm.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: A primary pneumothorax with a rim < 2 cm in a patient who is not breathless usually resolves without intervention.
whyNot: Aspiration is for breathless patients or a rim ≥ 2 cm.
A drain is reserved for failed aspiration, secondary or bilateral pneumothorax, or instability.
Decompression is for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise.
Surgery is for persistent air leak or recurrence.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites has a large right-sided transudative effusion. His medical therapy is being optimised.
questions.leadIn: Which intervention should generally be avoided?
options: Insertion of an intercostal chest drain
questions.explanation: In hepatic hydrothorax, the aim is to reduce the ascites and the pressure gradient. Chest tubes should be avoided. Repeated taps, TIPS or surgery are second-line, and transplant is definitive.
whyNot: This reduces ascites and is first-line.
As-needed taps are acceptable for symptoms.
TIPS is an option when medical therapy fails.
Transplant is definitive treatment.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman's chest X-ray shows a well-defined round opacity in the right mid-zone. She is known to have heart failure with bilateral effusions, and the opacity disappears after diuresis.
questions.leadIn: What did the opacity most likely represent?
questions.explanation: Fluid trapped in an oblique fissure can form a rounded opacity that mimics a tumour. Disappearance with diuresis gives it away.
whyNot: A tumour would not vanish with diuretics.
A subpulmonary effusion mimics a raised hemidiaphragm, not a mid-zone mass.
An empyema would not clear with diuretics and comes with sepsis.
Plaques are fixed and often calcified.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had a poorly treated right empyema for several weeks. He suddenly coughs up large volumes of purulent sputum. The chest X-ray now shows a horizontal air-fluid level within the right pleural space.
questions.leadIn: What complication has occurred?
questions.explanation: Pus under pressure has ruptured into a bronchus, causing a bronchopleural fistula with pyopneumothorax (air-fluid level) and copious purulent sputum. This needs surgery.
whyNot: Empyema necessitans is pus tracking out through the chest wall.
This follows rapid drainage of a large effusion.
Chyle is milky lymph, not pus.
Tension causes haemodynamic collapse and tracheal shift, not purulent sputum.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has periorbital and leg oedema, proteinuria of 7 g/day and a serum albumin of 18 g/L. He has small bilateral effusions with a fluid protein of 12 g/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the mechanism of these effusions?
options: Impaired pleural lymphatic drainage from tumour
Raised pulmonary venous pressure from left heart failure
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome lowers serum albumin and oncotic pressure, producing bilateral transudates. A low fluid protein confirms a transudate.
whyNot: Increased permeability produces exudates.
Lymphatic obstruction from tumour gives exudates.
Raised hydrostatic pressure is the heart-failure mechanism; nothing here suggests heart failure.
Thoracic duct obstruction gives chylothorax.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews malignant pleural effusions sent over a year.
questions.leadIn: Which primary tumour is the most common source?
questions.explanation: Lung cancer causes most malignant effusions (~36%), followed by breast (~25%) and lymphoma (~10%).
whyNot: Breast is the second commonest source.
Lymphoma is third.
Ovarian tumours are a less common source.
Mesothelioma is a primary pleural cancer and much rarer.

questions.stem: A student examines a patient with a large right pleural effusion and listens carefully at the upper border of the dull area.
questions.leadIn: Which sound may be heard just above the fluid level?
options: Normal vesicular breathing with increased vocal resonance over the fluid
questions.explanation: Lung compressed above an effusion can produce bronchial breathing or crackles at the upper border, while the fluid itself is silent.
whyNot: A pericardial rub is synchronous with the heartbeat, not a pleural sign.
Generalised wheeze suggests airway disease.
Vocal resonance is reduced, not increased, over fluid.
Stridor arises from the upper airway.

questions.stem: A pleural fluid sample is being classified using Light's criteria.
questions.leadIn: Which threshold defines an exudate for the pleural fluid : serum protein ratio?
questions.explanation: The protein ratio criterion is > 0.5. The LDH ratio criterion is > 0.6, and the fluid LDH must be > two-thirds of the ULN of serum LDH.
whyNot: 0.3 is too low.
0.6 is the LDH ratio threshold, not the protein one.
0.8 is not a Light's threshold.
1.0 is not a Light's threshold.

ospe.identify: Large right pleural effusion: stony dullness, absent breath sounds, trachea central or pushed away. On the X-ray inset the effusion hides the right heart border.
Pleural effusion on ultrasound: echo-free (black) fluid above the diaphragm with a positive "spine sign".
Large pleural effusion on chest X-ray: a dense, homogeneous shadow over part of the hemithorax with a meniscus on the erect film.
Loculated empyema: a D-shaped pleural-based opacity in the left mid-zone that persists despite a chest drain.
Septated pleural collection on ultrasound: multiloculated empyema.
Calcified asbestos pleural plaques with a "candle wax" outline on the diaphragm and lateral pleura (benign, asymptomatic).
